rows.answer: In a one-dimensional array, a peak is a local property where an element is greater than or equal to the elements to its left and right [1]. For example, position 2 is a peak if and only if $b \ge a$ and $b \ge c$ [1][5]. For elements located at the edges, one only needs to look to one side [3]; for instance, position 9 is a peak if $i \ge h$ [3][5].

In the case where the definition of a peak uses "greater than or equal to," any array will always have a peak [1]. However, if the definition were changed to "greater than," this argument cannot be made [1].

The straightforward peak finding algorithm starts from the left and walks across the array [2][3]. In the worst case, this algorithm requires a constant times $n$ [1], resulting in a linear asymptotic complexity of $\theta(n)$ [1][6].

The time complexity of the 1D divide and conquer peak finder is $\Theta(\log_2(n))$ [1], which is also referred to as $\log n$ complexity [3]. This is based on the recurrence $T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(1)$ [1].

An element $a$ is a 2D-peak if and only if $a \ge b, a \ge d, a \ge c, a \ge e$ [6]. Specifically, an element $(i, j)$ is a 2D peak if it is the maximum element in its column (meaning it has been compared to all adjacent elements looking up and down) and is also greater than or equal to the elements to its left $(i, j-1)$ and right $(i, j+1)$ [2].
The greedy ascent algorithm for 2D peak finding has a complexity of $\Theta(nm)$ [1][2][3]. In cases where $m = n$, the complexity is $\Theta(n^2)$ [1][2][3].

Finding a 1D peak in the middle column does not guarantee a 2D peak because, as seen in "Attempt #1" of the 2D peak finding problem, a 2D peak may not exist on the row $i$ where that 1D peak was found [3]. Consequently, this algorithm is incorrect [6].

The running time for the algorithm that picks the middle column and finds its global maximum (referred to as Attempt #2) is $\Theta(n \log m)$, where $n$ is the number of rows and $m$ is the number of columns [3]. If $m = n$, the complexity is $\Theta(n \log n)$ [3]. This is derived from the recurrence relation $T(n, m) = T(n, m/2) + \Theta(n)$, where $\Theta(n)$ is the work required to find the global maximum on a column [3].

The word "algorithm" comes from Al-Kharazmi (also spelled Al-Khwārizmī), who is considered the "father of algebra" [3][4]. He wrote a book titled "The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing" [3][4].

The Random Access Machine (RAM) is a theoretical model of computation [1][2][5]. It models Random Access Memory as a big array [2][3][4] organized by machine words [4].

The RAM model has the following characteristics:
*   **Structure**: It consists of $\Theta(1)$ registers, each of which is one word [2][3]. A word $w$ is $\ge \lg(\text{memory size})$ bits, and it is assumed that basic objects, such as integers, fit in a word [3].
*   **Capabilities**: In $\Theta(1)$ time, the model can [3]:
    *   Load a word at $r_i$ into register $r_j$ [3].
    *   Store register $r_j$ into memory at $r_i$ [3].
    *   Perform computations on registers, specifically $(+, -, *, /, \&, |, \wedge)$ [3].
*   **Access**: Because it is modeled as an array, any element can be accessed in constant time if its location is known [4].

The RAM is considered a realistic and powerful model [3][6] that is designed to be simple so that it is clear that operations take constant time [5].

A pointer machine is a model of computation that corresponds to a simple version of object-oriented programming [1]. It is characterized by the following:

*   **Objects and Fields:** It uses dynamically allocated objects [1][5]. Each object has a constant number of fields ($O(1)$ fields) [1][2][5]. A field can be either a word—such as an integer, a counter, or a computed value—or a pointer (also known as a reference) that points to another object or has a special value of null, nil, or none [1][5].
*   **Operations and Costs:** Manipulating an object with a constant number of attributes takes constant time [2]. The model supports dynamic memory allocation, allowing for the creation and destruction of nodes [4].
*   **Constraints:** Unlike pointers in C, pointers in a pointer machine cannot be "touched," meaning one cannot add to a pointer to move to the next item [4].
*   **Relationship to RAM:** The pointer machine is weaker than the Random Access Memory (RAM) model and can be implemented on a RAM, where a pointer is treated as an index into a giant table [4][5].

An example of a data structure in a pointer machine is a doubly linked list, which consists of nodes with fields for a value and pointers to the previous and next elements [3].

Appending an item to a Python list takes $\theta(1)$ time [4], which is constant time [2]. While allocating a new array and copying all elements would take linear time, Python does not use that method [1]; instead, it achieves $\theta(1)$ time via table doubling [4].

Document distance is defined based on shared words [2][3]. A document $D$ is treated as a vector where $D[w]$ represents the number of occurrences of a word $W$ in that document [2][3].

An initial attempt to define document distance is not scale invariant, which results in long documents with 99% of the same words appearing farther apart than short documents with 10% of the same words [1][3]. This is corrected by normalizing by the number of words $|D_i|$ in document $i$ [1][3]. 

Geometrically, this distance is interpreted as the angle between the vectors, defined as $d(D_1, D_2) = \arccos(d//(D_1, D_2))$ [1]. In this measure, an angle of $0^\circ$ means the documents are identical, while an angle of $90^\circ$ means they share no common words [1][4].

Insertion sort works by iterating through an input array and inserting each element into its correct position [1]. For $j \leftarrow 2$ to $n$, the algorithm inserts the key $A[j]$ into the sub-array $A[1 \dots j-1]$, which is already sorted [5]. This insertion is performed using pairwise swaps [1][3]. For example, if a key is 3, it will be swapped with elements such as 6, 5, and 4 until it is greater than the preceding element, such as 2 [3]. The algorithm requires $\Theta(1)$ constant auxiliary space, as it only needs a temporary variable to swap two elements [2].

Using binary search in insertion sort reduces the number of comparisons to $\Theta(n \log n)$ [1][2][3]. However, it does not make the overall running time $\Theta(n \log n)$ because, when using an array structure, inserting an element into the correct position requires shifting elements to the right [2][3]. This shifting process takes $\Theta(n)$ time in the worst case [1][2], meaning the complexity for swaps remains $\Theta(n^2)$ [2][4].

The merge step in merge sort combines two sorted arrays (such as $L'$ and $R'$ of size $n/2$) into a single sorted array of size $n$ [1]. This is accomplished using a "two-finger algorithm" that intersperses or interleaves the elements from the two sorted arrays [5]. The process involves using a couple of pointers to "walk up" the two arrays [2]. The complexity of this merge routine is $\Theta(n)$ [3][5].
Merge sort requires $\Theta(n)$ auxiliary space in order to perform the recursion and then place the results into the sorted array A [2].

The running time of merge sort is $\Theta(n \log n)$ [2][4]. This can be seen in the following ways:

*   **Recurrence and Recursion Tree:** Merge sort is a divide and conquer algorithm with a merge step that takes $\Theta(n)$ time [2][5]. This results in the recurrence $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn$, where $c > 0$ is a constant [5]. When analyzed using a recursion tree, there are $n$ leaves and an equal amount of work is done at each level, leading to a total complexity of $\Theta(n \lg n)$ [5].
*   **Intuition:** The result can be understood through a "proof by picture," which helps provide intuition behind why the result is true [2].
